lesson.title: dx: The Step You Get to Choose
lesson.summary: dx is simply the name for Delta x once differentials are in play, a freely chosen input step that is always exact, unlike dy, which is only an approximation of the true output change.
lesson.body:
It would be reasonable to ask why calculus bothers introducing the symbol dx at all, instead of just reusing Delta x everywhere. The answer is consistency: once dy is defined for the output of a function, giving the input step its own matching differential symbol, dx, lets the equation dy = f'(x) dx read as a single coherent statement about two paired differentials, rather than mixing an old symbol with a new one.

There is also a deeper reason dx earns its own name instead of just being Delta x in disguise. Consider the simplest possible function, y = x itself. Its derivative is 1 everywhere, so applying the differential definition gives dy = f'(x) dx = 1 * dx = dx. In other words, for the independent variable, the differential and the actual change are the very same number, with zero approximation gap, because y = x is already a straight line and linearization of a straight line is exact. That is precisely why it is safe to call the input step dx: for x itself, dx and Delta x are identical, not merely close.

This contrasts sharply with dy for a dependent variable. In the previous chapter's example, y = x^2 at x = 3 with a step of 0.1, dx was exactly 0.1, matching Delta x exactly by definition, no approximation involved. But dy came out to 0.6, only approximately equal to the true change Delta y = 0.61. So dx is always exact, because it is simply the input you chose; dy is generally only approximate, because it is a prediction computed from that input using the slope f'(x).

In dy = f'(x) dx, then, dx should be read as the independent variable in the equation: pick any value you like for it, and dy is whatever falls out as a consequence.
